hints: Count paths if there were no traps using combinations.
Sort the traps and subtract paths according to the first trap they hit.
Treat the destination as one extra point after all traps.
analogy: Count all monotone routes, then remove those that first step onto a forbidden square.
example: On a 3 by 3 grid there are 6 paths. If (2,2) is a trap, four pass through it, leaving 2.
algorithm: Sort traps by row and column and append destination (n,n). For each point p, start with C(row+col-2,row-1), the number of paths from (1,1). For each earlier trap t with both coordinates no larger than p, subtract ways[t]*C((p.row-t.row)+(p.col-t.col),p.row-t.row). Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo 1000000007. The destination value is the answer.
correctness: Every monotone path to p either avoids earlier traps or has a unique first trap. The stored ways[t] count paths whose first trap is t, and the binomial coefficient counts all continuations to p. Subtracting those disjoint classes leaves exactly trap-free paths.
complexity: For grid size n and m traps, time is O(n+m^2) and space O(n+m), assuming factorials through 2n are precomputed.
